title: Downtown building heights plan approved with changes
subtitle: Also: Stone Road and Edinburgh Road planning permits, Clair Road townhouses, Frost Building designation deferred, heritage designations.
overview: Council approved the Downtown Heights Study Official Plan Amendment, which sets how tall buildings can be across downtown, after making a series of changes {{vote:m28}}. Council kept the Norfolk/Woolwich corridor at 2-4 storeys until a heritage conservation district study is done, restored wider view corridors to the Basilica, and capped the west side of Gordon Street south of Waterloo Avenue at six storeys. Proposals to lower heights on the Police Station and Armouries lands, and along Woolwich Street, were defeated.

Council also asked staff to report back on ways to encourage higher energy standards for tall buildings, and approved a Community Planning Permit System for the Stone Road and Edinburgh Road area {{vote:m32}}. The system combines zoning, minor variance and site plan approvals into one process with a 45-day decision period. Council approved the official plan and zoning changes for 62 stacked townhouses at 132 Clair Road West {{vote:m29}}.

Council deferred designating the Frost Building at 328 Victoria Road South under the Ontario Heritage Act until the Guelph Innovation District block plan comes forward, no later than March 31, 2026 {{vote:m31}}. Eight consent items began the heritage designation process for properties on Paisley Street, Glasgow Street North and Eramosa Road. After a closed session, the Mayor reported that Council gave staff direction on an Ontario Land Tribunal matter at 895 and 919 York Road and on a proposed employment land acquisition.

decisions.item: Downtown Heights Study Official Plan Amendment
decisions.detail: Council approved the amended official plan amendment (OPA 106) changing permitted building heights in the Downtown Secondary Plan area {{vote:m28}}.
The Norfolk/Woolwich corridor from Oxford to Edwin stays at 2-4 storeys until a heritage conservation district study is completed {{vote:m15}}.
The west side of Gordon Street between Waterloo Avenue and Surrey Street West was reduced to a maximum of 6 storeys {{vote:m25}}.
View corridors to the Basilica were changed: Gordon Street returns to the January 2025 version and Macdonell Street is protected edge to edge from Wellington to Norfolk {{vote:m20}}.
Urban Design Master Plans and matching zoning amendments may make minor adjustments to boundaries between height areas, while keeping the Basilica view corridors {{vote:m12}}.

decisions.item: Stone Road and Edinburgh Road planning permits
decisions.detail: Council approved a Community Planning Permit System for the Stone Road/Edinburgh Road growth area, with related by-law and reserve fund policy changes {{vote:m32}}.
Council approved the official plan and zoning amendments to allow 62 stacked townhouses at 132 Clair Road West {{vote:m29}}.
Council deferred the notice of intention to designate the Frost Building until the Guelph Innovation District block plan is presented, and no later than March 31, 2026 {{vote:m31}}.

debate: Delegates were split on the height study. A development consultant and a realtors' association spokesperson praised it as a balanced, bold plan for housing supply. One resident delegate questioned water and sewer capacity, parkland, parking and development charge costs. Another delegate wanted lower heights on the west side of Gordon Street to ease the shift to a low-rise neighbourhood.

Developers sought changes. One wanted more height on a triangular site. Another asked for flexibility at height-zone boundaries, which staff supported and Council adopted. The same delegate argued that treating rooftop mechanical penthouses as part of the permitted height was heavy-handed and needed more study. A councillor later raised the same concern, and Council amended the policy.

Councillors who backed heritage protections argued that once height is permitted, land assembly follows, and most of the Norfolk/Woolwich buildings are not yet protected. Opponents said the blanket 2-4 storey limit would block development for years and that existing heritage processes already apply. On the Police Station and Armouries lands, opponents said the site had room for housing near transit.

On energy, staff said the city cannot require higher standards beyond the building code and that a report would need staff time. Supporters wanted options to encourage stronger standards. One councillor opposed exploring a ban on new gas hookups, so Council voted on the two parts separately.

On the Frost Building, the owner's representatives asked to review the building together with the block plan. Staff said the block plan would take until later in 2025 and were comfortable with the deferral. On the planning permit system, one councillor raised limited third-party appeal rights, and staff said site plan approvals already have none. Staff also said the pilot would be monitored and refined, and they responded to home builders' concerns.
